title: Re: Issue #11523 Removal of XSLT from the web platform
body:
*** Re: Issue #11523 Removal of XSLT from the web platform

As I was debugging an XSLT Stylesheet for my GitHub project last week I received the notice from GitHub in the Browser Diagnostic Tools that XSLT was deprecated and will be removed from browsers in 2026.  Since that time I have been trying to understand the process that led to this decision, and the path forward for me, and likely others like me. I am still looking for solid answers. 

Most concerning of all is that this issue has not been advertised or discussed in a public forum. GitHub knows the makeup of my project as shown below... I should have been notified in October, long before this decision was finalized.  

Discussion... 
Client Side XSLT is the perfect solution for what I am doing. Enabled by static html pages on GitHub, it's browser agnostic and it's standards based. 

The rationale presented in "Should we remove XSLT from the web platform? #11523 [(https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11523)](url) sound like arguments of convenience. They do not present a business value argument. They are not compelling.

Downloads argument...** #11523 says..."a significant [decline](https://chromestatus.com/metrics/feature/timeline/popularity/78) in the use of client-side XSLT. Its role within the web browser has been largely superseded by JavaScript-based technologies such as JSON+React." Indeed there are additional options, but that is not a rationale. By that metric, my project is worthless... it contains 4.6% CSS, 5.8% XSLT, 88.8% JavaScript, and 0.8% other.  99% of the JavaScript is loaded from open source.  100% of the XSLT is coded by me. The rationale did not quantify the impact of removing an option away with short notice and no a migration path. The impact to me is that the project becomes a doorstop if/when XSLT goes away.  Likely others are severely impacted as well.  

Security Vulnerabilities argument... CVE.ORG shows 112 total registered vulnerabilities for XSLT for all recorded time. There were none in 2026 and five in 2025. In contrast, 7687 vulnerabilities have been registered for JavaScript, with more than 50 to date in 2026. So from that basis, logic supports removing JavaScript...

The business value argument needs to include: cost, time, and loss of function. 

Ironically, my small GitHub project is security related (which is listed as an issue for eliminating XSLT. [https://jjwhitmore.github.io/SE-workbench/ ](url). The tools allow the users to investigate a range of security issues and perspectives on their local platform. The tools easily show 36 variants of JavaScript attacks. Google Analytics shows that the project has been used by more than 450 users from 40 countries. 

For your consideration, and the consideration of the Issue #11523 collaborators... my suggestion would be to pause the deprecation of XSLT until the true impact can be investigated, look into whether XSLT can be packaged browser plug-ins, run the plug-in in a sandbox, and then focus on bulletproofing JavaScript.
